adds.title: Outright International: Mozambique country page
adds.summary: Thin: no usable prison-housing finding. Outright's Mozambique overview (updated March 2026) covers decriminalised same-sex conduct (2015 penal code), absence of any legal gender-recognition procedure, and social barriers for LGBTIQ people, but contains no information on where transgender prisoners are housed, no placement rule, and no documented custody case involving a trans person.

adds.title: Mozambique: Events of 2023 (HRW World Report 2024)
adds.summary: Thin: no usable prison-housing finding. The HRW World Report 2024 Mozambique chapter (published 11 Jan 2024) documents general police detentions and election-related arrests but contains no transgender-specific content and no prison-placement information for trans prisoners.

records.note: No prison-housing data found for Mozambique: in the Wikipedia full-text search, Outright International's country page, and the HRW World Report country chapter, no rule or documented case locating where transgender prisoners are housed (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, or segregation practice) was found. Mozambique has no legal gender-recognition procedure, so a formal placement-by-registered-sex rule is plausible, but no source located confirms prison practice.

adds.title: Rwanda's transgender community face violent detentions for being trans (VICE World News)
adds.summary: VICE World News (20 Nov 2020): although being transgender is not criminalised in Rwanda, police routinely arrest trans women on pretext charges — 'homelessness', drug sales, theft — and detain them at Kigali's Gikondo Transit Center, a facility for people exhibiting 'deviant acts or behaviors'. Bella was held there after police falsely claimed she was homeless and sold drugs; as punishment she was confined in a tiny dark cell known as 'the cat box' and raped by fellow detainees at least three times. Gabi was detained at Gikondo for six months in 2018; Nunu was detained there three times between 2018 and 2019. Detainees are supposed to be charged within 72 hours or transferred to a police station, court, rehabilitation facility, or jail, but trans detainees are held for indeterminate periods in facilities lacking transparency. Documents placement practice: trans prisoners are held under a 'deviance rehabilitation' framework in transit centres (with segregated/confining cells used as punishment), not in facilities matching their gender identity.

adds.title: Outright International: Rwanda country page
adds.summary: Thin-to-useful: Outright's Rwanda page (updated March 2026, based on a July 2025 Human Rights First Rwanda Association submission to the UN Human Rights Committee) reports transgender individuals face heightened risks of harassment at identity checks and arbitrary arrests on grounds such as 'vagrancy' or 'public order' offenses, and that LGBTIQ people flee arbitrary arrests, detention and ill-treatment. It corroborates the detention pattern for trans people but gives no prison-placement (men's vs women's facility) detail.

records.note: Rwanda's documented practice for trans people in custody is arrest on pretext 'vagrancy'/'public order'/deviance grounds and detention in Kigali's Gikondo Transit Center, a 'rehabilitation' facility where trans women face abusive conditions including confinement in a punishment cell ('the cat box'), rape by fellow detainees, and indeterminate stays (VICE, 20 Nov 2020; corroborated by Outright International's account of arbitrary arrests per a July 2025 UN Human Rights Committee submission). No statutory rule on placement by birth sex vs gender identity, and no special transgender housing unit, was found; no authority was located that places trans prisoners in facilities matching their gender identity.
